Author: Colin Meloy
My Review: I enjoyed the ride that this second installment has taken me on. Of course the narrative did not end neatly, as it’s part of a trilogy. I think that the author broke up the books in a smart way to keep me wanting more. To be continued.

Title: Kissing Kosher
Author: Jean Meltzer
My Review: I read this on a whim and was surprised by how sensitive and creative a romance book could be. This is my second book that I’ve read by this author and I love the way that she incorporates her protagonist’s chronic illnesses into the narratives. The topics of babka, marijuana, dietary restrictions and love helped to elevate this Romeo and Juliet style romance to something unique and hilarious.

Title: The Matzah Ball
Author: Jean Meltzer

Title: Wildwood (Wildwood Chronicles, #1)
Author: Colin Meloy
My Review: This book, wonderfully Narnia-esque, satisfied my craving for a little mystery, fantasy and frolicking with nature. Finishing the book, made me wonder what's next for my new friends Prue and Curtis? It goes without saying that the illustrations lofted the book to a shelf filled with Alice in Wonderland, Narnia and Harry Potter. Not bad company, if I do say so. Read it with a cup of hot chocolate in your favorite chair in the house.

Title: Adventures from the Land of Stories: The Mother Goose Diaries / Queen Red Riding Hood's Guide to Royalty
Author: Chris Colfer
Publisher: Little, Brown Books for Young Readers
My Review: This set of epistolary tales from the pens of Red Riding Hood and Mother Goose was an excellent audiobook read dramatically by Chris Colfer. I enjoyed the Red Riding Hood story more than the Mother Goose one. Red incorporated funny storytelling and a rethinking of her story while Mother just reminded me a bit of Forest Gump (in this case Mother Goose is Mr. Gump). Nevertheless it was entertaining and my 8 year old son and I enjoyed listening to it together.

My Review: I appropriately found this book in a Little Free Library on the Upper East Side of Manhattan. This unique epistolary was such a page turner that I felt as though I had been on the mail exchange.

My Review: As always, Tim Probert produced an amazingly beautiful adventure story for us. Every page was jaw droppingly gorgeous. This installment of the series felt, as the title would suggest, as in between before and after something juicy was really about to happen. The book built my appetite for what’s to come in the future and it made me long for some of the earlier stories where the group of friends had more time together. More than a narrative, the story produced a mood. Mood where people were trying to find themselves and figuring out what’s in store for the next.

Title: Playful: How Play Shifts Our Thinking, Inspires Connection, and Sparks Creativity
Author: Cas Holman
My Review: I enjoyed reading this manifesto of sorts on having a playful mindset. The stories that Holman provides are joyous and invite the reader to figure out what play means on their own terms.

Author: Daniel Immerwahr

Title: The Shadow of the Wind (The Cemetery of Forgotten Books, #1)
Author: Carlos Ruiz Zafón
My Review: This is how books are supposed to be written. It felt like a book I just had to hold in my hands. The plot had so many stories and sub-plots attached to it that it felt like an extremely satisfying and well-written soap opera. This was not a quick read and I found myself luxuriating in the well crafted world that he created.

Title: Into the Bewilderness
Author: Gus Gordon
My Review:
This story felt like a walk on an autumn day.

The story of two friends traveling to the big city by foot and then by bus, is smart and well drawn. I wish the city part was described in more detail, it felt a bit rushed.

Title: Atlas of the Heart: Mapping Meaningful Connection and the Language of Human Experience
Author: Brené Brown

Title: Crying in H Mart
Author: Michelle Zauner

Title: The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why It Matters
Author: Priya Parker
My Review: I’ve enjoyed the journey of reading this book about gathering. Like the title suggests, the book explores the anatomy of meetings,events, parties and moments of connection.  Parker methodically dissects an event from the moment you conceive of it through to the weeks after it has ended. The Product Designer in me luxuriated in all of these moments of designed triangulation. I know the lessons I’ve learned along the way will resonate for some time.

Title: My Brilliant Life
Author: Kim Ae-ran

Title: Sheets (Sheets, #1)
Author: Brenna Thummler
My Review: This is a quiet story about a lonely girl and equally lonely ghost who connect in a laundromat. The drawings are beautiful and the story has a sweetness to it. Parts of the plot felt rushed . The best parts of this book were the quiet and slow moments that allowed you to savor the story.

Title: Dear Sophie, Love Sophie: A Graphic Memoir in Diaries, Letters, and Lists―A Unique and Witty Reflection on Relationships, Identity, and Belonging
Author: Sophie Lucido Johnson
My Review: I’ve recommended this book to many people. I love the general concept of having conversations with different versions of yourself crossing the barriers of time and reality. The writing is authentic and doesn’t sugar coat life experiences.

Title: Sorceline. Book 2 (#4-5)
Author: Sylvia Douyé
My Review: I enjoyed the story, however I felt like there was a lot of plot dumping in this second installment.  I wish that the author showed big chunks of the characters and their backstories. Other than that I love this dark world and am ready to sink my teeth (in a vampire like way) in to book 3.

My Review: Wr read this one after dinner one night as a family and it did not disappoint. It was cozy and unexpectedly witty. The drawings are hysterical and I don’t want to say any more because I will certainly spoil it.

Title: Stone Fruit
Author: Lee Lai
My Review: The way that the author throws you into the lives of the different families  of the story is both authentic and familiar. The artwork is drop dead gorgeous.

Title: Sorceline Book 1 (#1-3)
Author: Sylvia Douyé
My Review: I was drawn to the book because of the beautiful illustrations but the story is compelling. It has many similar themes to other stories in this genre - group of teens who are at a school because of their magical powers, however the way that the author reveals information and paces the story is unique and well, magical.

The artwork was beautiful (a touch reminiscent of Stephen Collins (The Gigantic Beard That Was Evil)). I gave 4 not 5 stars because the story felt like it tied up a bit too tidy. Overall a fun story with a batch of well thought through characters and scenes.

I listened to this as an audiobook and really appreciated how the narrator was able to capture the different perspectives and voices of the women depicted in the story. A decidedly feminist apothecary drew me into her world of healing and poisoning. The end of the story dragged on a touch but it’s still worth a read.

I loved every all the side quests that he goes through during this q and a formatted biography.

Title: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (Harry Potter, #1)
Author: J.K. Rowling
My Review: I re-read this book recently with my son. I was still captured by the magical wizarding world and loved seeing how my son reacted to it. I was really excited to read a book that featured a smart and kind male protagonist. In the early chapters the protagonist and his newly acquired best friend are pretty horrible to their only substantial female friend. It was difficult to read those parts out loud but redemption came when they later become friends and miss her when she is out of the room. I feel like there’s a larger conversation about gender and friendship here, but I’ll leave that for another day.

My Review: I feel like I just got back after spending a year with a good friend in Jerusalem. It was such a beautiful and delicate read. I loved all of the moments of attempting to create while also managing the day to day life of a parent. Reading this now while there is so much happen politically wasn’t intentional but it made the experience that much more meaningful.

Title: The Dictionary of Lost Words
Author: Pip Williams
My Review: The first bit of the book was fascinating and I could not put it down. I wanted to learn of this top secret society of people who compile the dictionary. In fact, it reminded me of many of the issues that are encountered in present day for Wikipedia editors. At one point however, it felt like the author could not figure out how to end the story. Characters died, the narrator completely changed and the story felt abruptly ended.

My Review: Really sweet book with creative illustrations and graphics. Definitely one to read with your partner,bestie or other half while sitting on a couch and drinking hot coco.

My Review: I deeply enjoyed the journey of the first 3/4 of the narrative. The worlds that she has created are so vivid and beautifully described that I felt as though I had entered them myself. I was a bit disappointed with the ending, the character development fell a bit flat, new characters were introduced and the conclusion was unsatisfying.

Author: Susanna Clarke
My Review: I enjoyed the journey of exploring the world crafted by Clarke in Piranesi. The labyrinth or house inhabited by the protagonist was so vividly described that it acted as an unique character in itself. I  appreciate that I had no clear idea where the story would take me at any given point. Ultimately the way that the themes of memory and trusting in yourself and others emerged were touching and unforgettable (pun intended). I didn’t want the adventure to end and when it did, it felt like leaving a sacred space.

My Review: After everything that Trevor Noah has been through, it's hard to imagine that he has an established career as a comedian. His words are earnest, playful and smart. His biography talks about his relationship with his mother, his community in Cape Town and growing up and living life as a biracial child in Apartheid South Africa.  While his humor colors every bit of writing, his story is heartbreaking.

Author: Sara Wachter-Boettcher
My Review: This should be required reading for every person in tech. As a designer, I found the use cases that she described insightful. The tools that she provided to shield yourself from the common pitfalls of algorithmic failure are practical and clever.

Title: Unlimited: How to Build an Exceptional Life
Author: Jillian Michaels
My Review: I listed to this entire audio book while working out and it was very inspiring. I recommend the audio version because you can hear her voice and words simultaneously. While it is a self help book, the tools that she offers can be applied to any discipline for setting and achieving goals.

Title: Becoming
Author: Michelle Obama
My Review: I listened to this as an audiobook. I highly recommend this format because Michelle Obama is a great storyteller. This book was thoughtful and inspiring. I listened to it every day from the second that I started it.

Title: The Fat Cat: A Danish Folktale
Author: Jack Kent
My Review: This is a tale of a serial killer who went around town eating everything and everyone in sight only to meet his demise when he encounters the local axe wielding woodcutter.

Title: The Sun Also Rises
Author: Ernest Hemingway
My Review: I kept imagining myself as part of the protagonist's ex-pat cohort, sitting at coffee shops and bars. In this classic Hemingway perfectly describes the excitement of learning about cultures, love, and traditions through travel. His characteristic economic use of language satisfyingly compliments the narrative experience.  Understandably this is book is a product of its time, however, I was taken a back by the overt anti-semitism in the book.

Title: Skim
Author: Mariko Tamaki

Title: Calamity and Other Stories
Author: Daphne Kalotay
My Review: The quiet short stories are comforting. I felt like I was able to really understand and empathize with this collection of interwoven stories and characters

Title: The Girl with All the Gifts (The Girl With All the Gifts, #1)
Author: M.R. Carey
My Review: This book was very different than my typical reads, but I found myself returning to it every night with enthusiasm. There were parts that went slower than others , but in almost a cinematic cadence. Although this story is filled with gore and fighting, at its heart it is about a young girl coming into her own and figuring out how to mobilize and navigate her emotions within the world.

Title: The Diamond as Big as the Ritz
Author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
My Review: This impeccably written short story was simultaneously beautiful and uncomfortable.

Title: Creativity, Inc.: Overcoming the Unseen Forces That Stand in the Way of True Inspiration
Author: Ed Catmull

Title: This One Summer
Author: Mariko Tamaki
My Review: This is my second book by the Jillian/ Mariko Tamaki team. These dark coming of age stories capture a period of time filled with delightful meanderings and touching conversations between family and friends. I couldn't put the book down, I was so enthralled with this moment in these two friends' lives and the beautifully depicted and moody illustrations.

Title: The Alchemist
Author: Paulo Coelho
My Review: The only book that I can compare this reading experience to is The Little Prince. It's the kind of book where you find yourself lingering on each sentence, wondering about the depth of the meaning behind each vivid image that has been so delicately described. I felt sad when the book ended because that meant I had to stop reading it - what more of a compliment could an author ask for?

Author: Diana Gabaldon
My Review: I read this book after watching the series on Starz. It was a pure treat luxuriating in the language, history and well researched details. The best time travel-romance-action book I've ever read!

Title: The Elements of Content Strategy
Author: Erin Kissane
My Review: This was the first book that I've ever read on Content Strategy and I think that it served it's purpose.  The book dissected expectations of the content strategist and explained how and where the discipline interacts with related processes such as user experience and information architecture. Additionally, Kissane has a wonderfully with writing voice and has many valuable anecdotal insights and references.

Title: Going Responsive
Author: Karen Mcgrane
My Review: This is a great overview as to how responsive web design needs to be a team mindset rather than a "project."  With practical tips and exercises, I found that this book acted as a reference tool for explaining different concepts to my colleagues. Parts of the book left me wanting more - and the author referenced other places to receive that content so the resulting book felt more like a rwd 101 or survey class. Overall I would recommend this to anyone working on the web today.

Title: Design Is a Job
Author: Mike Monteiro
My Review: This book should be required reading for every designer. I would just hand this to students when they get their art school diplomas. With his snark and years of practical experience in the field, Design is a Job has been sharply crafted by Mike Monteiro to help designers to feel empowered in their work.  He does this by mobilizing you with tips, tools and best practices that are presented in a confident "balls out" manner.  I enjoyed the chapter on feedback the most as it articulated a framework for teaching clients how to provide you with actionable critique.

Author: David Kadavy

Author: Yolanda Pettinato
My Review: Nice beginner book about all of the basic yoga poses.

Title: Ordering Disorder: Grid Principles for Interaction Design
Author: Khoi Vinh
My Review: I have often looked for a book to help me conceptually wrap my brain around design frameworks for the Web and Ordering Disorder accomplished that (for the most part). Although Ordering Disorder was written in a period when fixed width layouts were more popular than responsive design, I still find this book useful as it is explaining some core design principles and practices that can be applied to many different kinds of mediums and design theory.

Title: El Deafo
Author: Cece Bell
My Review:
El Deafo is a semi-autobiographical story about CeCe Bell, the deaf author-illustrator of this wonderful graphic novel. I learned about this book after listening to this story on NPR interviewing the author : http://www.npr.org/2014/12/14/369599042/el-deafo-how-a-girl-turned-her-disability-into-a-superpower

While the story is about how this young girl navigates life after her hearing becomes impaired, the true heart of the story is capturing the feelings of a first crush, loneliness, feeling like an outsider and the joy of having a best friend. The story is heartwarming, relatable and funny. The illustrative style of CeCe Bell is wonderfully whimsical and perfectly matches the tone of the storytelling.

Title: Fantastic Mr. Fox
Author: Roald Dahl
My Review: I decided to read this book after many years of "meaning to" or plain assuming that I had already read it. The book was a wonderfully dark tale (and tail!) that followed the adventures of a family of foxes and fellow animal diggers that were stuck underground beneath three questionable farmers land. Although I knew the story from the movies, the way that the story was woven by Dahl remains magical and unmatched.

Title: The Gigantic Beard that Was Evil
Author: Stephen    Collins
My Review: I picked this up after having been seduced by the staggeringly beautiful and jaw dropping graphics at a my local comic book store. The Gigantic Beard That Was Evil was not only visually compelling, but it had a story that pulled me in from the first page. There was a perfect combination of character development and plot. I can easily imagine this story being adapted into an animation.

Title: Wild: From Lost to Found on the Pacific Crest Trail
Author: Cheryl Strayed
My Review: This book felt like the love child of Born To Run and Eat, Pray, Love. I truly soaked this book in over the past three days. It's a story that will inspire you to take a leap and to embrace yourself ... Warts and all. Strayed has a wonderfully approachable writing style that made this read enjoyable and memorable. Girl Power ftw

Title: Creative Confidence: Unleashing the Creative Potential Within Us All
Author: Tom Kelley
My Review: This book gave an excellent overview of the creative process behind IDEO as a way to incorporate strategies for having the grit and confidence to make change in your life (and hopefully the lives of others) through design. The book is filled with fantastic real world case studies as well as practical techniques - that explore the world far beyond  design firms. I particularly enjoyed the exercises at the end of the book that give you concrete ways to move forward and live a life filled with and informed by creative confidence.

Title: Bird by Bird
Author: Anne Lamott
My Review:
Lots of people who I admire love this book and swear by it, so I decided to read it on my summer vacation. While the book gives very practical tips about writing - like dedicating time to write every single day- really, this is a book about life and finding your own voice as you navigate the world.

I enjoyed the honest and funny writing.

Title: Is Everyone Hanging Out Without Me? (And Other Concerns)

Title: Don't Make Me Think: A Common Sense Approach to Web Usability
Author: Steve Krug
My Review: Admittedly, this is a book that every designer, developer and product manager I work with recommends. I decided to read this book because I wanted to read a book that gave me the nuts and bolts of web usability and this was in my "bucket list" of books to read before the world ends, and honestly, the book was the solution for all of my questions and usability needs. Don't Make Me Think does three things: 1. it explains the components of a usable site and how to use them 2. it teaches you how to user test and 3. it describes accessibility. I agree with the chorus of devs and designers - read the book and make some great, usable sites.

Title: New Jewish Wedding
Author: Anita Diamant
My Review: I am in the middle of planning my wedding and my rabbi recommended that my fiance and I read this book. The New Jewish Wedding provided a wealth of information on wedding rituals - traditional and new. The book is very informative and offers great historical context for pre-wedding, wedding day and post-wedding rituals, as well as practical information on implementation. I recommend reading this book so that you feel prepared for your wedding, and also know the meaning behind all of your actions and intentions with this commitment. The writing is simple, clean and beautiful.

Title: Participate: Designing with User-Generated Content
Author: Helen Armstrong
My Review: I could not stop turning the pages on this book. The writing guides you through maker and participatory culture through explanatory yet thought provoking essays. The essays are then paired with case studies that allow you to explore fine art, interactive design and DIY participatory investigations. This book has been by my side for the past two weeks in all of my meetings at my open source software design job. As our design culture progresses to become more participatory and collaborative, I suspect (and it is my not so secret hope) that the practices and techniques described in this book will become innate for individuals engaging in design.

Title: In the Beginning...Was the Command Line
Author: Neal Stephenson
My Review:
This book made me think. For sure, reading this in 2014 highlights how much has changed with the web, hardware and software - however, I recommend reading at least a few chapters of this to get a real sense for maker culture. Here you can sink your teeth into why certain choices were made for the design of operating systems, and for the n00bs (including myself) you learn along the way basic notions such as what the difference is between a hardware and software.

I gave this 3 stars - because it was a bit rough for me to power through. I found a lot of the references and metaphors to be unapologetically nerdy, which is fine, but just didn't totally resonate with me.

Title: Go
Author: Chip Kidd
My Review:
This book should be required reading for everyone - not everyone who wants to be a designer, or every child - but everyone who lives and breathes and participates in some form in the designed world. I found this book very satisfying, it provided clarity to many complex concepts with witty examples, playful exercises and intriguing factoids about the history of design.

I particularly appreciate the approach that Kidd takes for this subject matter. He doesn't overly focus on the medium of design but pays acute attention to the message that any given design is communicating.

My only criticism is that this book is clearly marketed and designed for youth - but seemingly written for an adult reader. I listened to an interview that Chip Kidd did with Debbie Millman on Design Matters about this - where he said that it was his secret plan to appeal to everyone with this book (a mission he certainly accomplished). But I found that many of his references were outdated and probably a bit obscure for a younger reader (he talked about Fred Flintstone). He did not down talk to the reader, which although I appreciate I found that at times he talked around the subject with other complex examples or metaphors. I would love to see how a 10 year old responds to this book.
